questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the strongest way to respond to the 'why not just point-to-point' objection against a middleware-hub design?
options: Insist middleware is always the better choice in every scenario
Refuse to answer the question since it challenges the chosen design

Concede that point-to-point is genuinely simpler for a single integration, then point at the specific tradeoff (maintenance cost across five-plus integrations) that justifies the hub for Doverfield's actual situation
Claim point-to-point integration is technically impossible in Salesforce
questions.explain: The strong answer partially concedes the objection's valid point before explaining the specific scale-driven tradeoff that makes the hub the right call for Doverfield's five-plus integrations specifically, not integrations in general.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend when a design genuinely has no good answer to a scaling objection like '10x data volume'?
options: Say so plainly, and name the specific change needed to close the gap, such as moving an object from scheduled incremental extract to CDC
Pretend the design already handles it without naming any specific change
Avoid answering the question entirely
Claim data volume never actually grows in real Salesforce orgs
questions.explain: An honest gap admission paired with a concrete fix is explicitly called out as a stronger answer than pretending a design handles something it doesn't.

questions.q: How does the strong answer to the 'single point of failure' objection about the IdP handle the objection, per this lesson?
options: By denying that the IdP is a dependency at all
By arguing that single points of failure never actually cause outages
By proposing to remove the IdP integration entirely on the spot
By naming the specific mitigation already built into the design -- keeping a non-SSO administrative login path available so an IdP outage doesn't lock out every user
questions.explain: The strong answer doesn't deny the dependency exists -- it names the concrete mitigation (the non-SSO fallback path from Lesson 3) that addresses the specific risk the objection raises.

questions.q: What does the fourth objection pattern in this lesson ('how do you know this works under failure') actually probe?
options: Whether the candidate can recite the retry-with-backoff pattern from memory
Whether the resilience patterns (retry/backoff, dead-letter queues, circuit breakers) were actually tested under failure conditions, or only designed and assumed to work
Whether the design uses Named Credentials
Whether the integration uses the Bulk API
questions.explain: This objection tests whether resilience was verified in practice (e.g., by actually taking an endpoint offline in a sandbox) rather than just designed on paper and assumed to behave correctly.

questions.q: Why does this lesson frame reviewer objections as 'the actual test' rather than attacks to be deflected?
options: Because objections are scored separately from the rest of the presentation and don't affect the overall evaluation
Because review boards are required to ask exactly four objections per candidate
Because they test whether the candidate's reasoning holds up under the same kind of pressure a real production incident or skeptical stakeholder would apply later
Because objections are randomly generated and unrelated to the actual design presented
questions.explain: The framing matters: objections exist to test whether the underlying reasoning is sound under pressure, which is exactly the posture a real architect needs when a stakeholder or incident challenges a design later.
